report.source_text: ADV was switched to entecavir at a dose of 1.0 mg every other day. Supplementation with oral phosphate products and vitamin D was continued for his hypophosphatemic osteomalacia. Oral sodium bicarbonate was also added for the treatment of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. The patient's hyperphosphatasemia, hypophosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis gradually improved, and his lower limb pain did not recur. His kidney function was almost unchanged, but the level of urinary β2-microglobulin remained high over the following two years (Figure). The pan-aminoaciduria, glycosuria, and hypouricemia were not completely ameliorated.

clinician.final_diagnosis: Adefovir dipivoxil (ADV)-induced Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphatemic osteomalacia
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 68-year-old Japanese man with type 2 diabetes and chronic HBV infection received ADV therapy (10 mg daily) starting June 2005 for lamivudine-resistant HBV. After 3 years of ADV exposure, kidney dysfunction was first noted in 2008 (creatinine 1.79 mg/dL). Over the subsequent 6 years, progressive proximal tubular dysfunction developed silently. In January 2014 (9 years after ADV initiation), the patient developed osteomalacia symptoms: muscle weakness, bilateral knee pain, and left plantar lesion. Four months before nephrology referral (approximately May 2016), osteomalacia was formally diagnosed. At nephrology referral in September 2016 (11 years of ADV exposure), comprehensive laboratory evaluation revealed classic Fanconi syndrome: hypophosphatemia (1.6 mg/dL) with phosphaturia (FePO4 79.3%), hypouricemia (1.6 mg/dL) with uricosuria (FUA 69.3%), normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (HCO3- 14.6), glycosuria (4+), pan-aminoaciduria, and markedly elevated urinary β2-microglobulin (66,919 μg/L). X-ray imaging (September 2015) confirmed osteomalacia with Looser zones in metatarsal bones and proximal tibias. ADV was discontinued and switched to entecavir 1.0 mg every other day, with supplementation of oral phosphate, vitamin D, and sodium bicarbonate. Following ADV discontinuation, hyperphosphatasemia, hypophosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis gradually improved, and lower limb pain resolved. However, urinary β2-microglobulin remained elevated over the 2-year follow-up, and kidney function remained largely unchanged, indicating irreversible tubular damage from prolonged ADV exposure.

final.final_diagnosis: Adefovir dipivoxil (ADV)-induced Fanconi syndrome with hypophosphatemic osteomalacia
final.trajectory_summary: A 68-year-old Japanese man with type 2 diabetes and chronic HBV infection received ADV therapy (10 mg daily) starting June 2005 for lamivudine-resistant HBV. After 3 years of ADV exposure, kidney dysfunction was first noted in 2008 (creatinine 1.79 mg/dL). Over the subsequent 6 years, progressive proximal tubular dysfunction developed silently. In January 2014 (9 years after ADV initiation), the patient developed osteomalacia symptoms: muscle weakness, bilateral knee pain, and left plantar lesion. Four months before nephrology referral (approximately May 2016), osteomalacia was formally diagnosed. At nephrology referral in September 2016 (11 years of ADV exposure), comprehensive laboratory evaluation revealed classic Fanconi syndrome: hypophosphatemia (1.6 mg/dL) with phosphaturia (FePO4 79.3%), hypouricemia (1.6 mg/dL) with uricosuria (FUA 69.3%), normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (HCO3- 14.6), glycosuria (4+), pan-aminoaciduria, and markedly elevated urinary β2-microglobulin (66,919 μg/L). X-ray imaging (September 2015) confirmed osteomalacia with Looser zones in metatarsal bones and proximal tibias. ADV was discontinued and switched to entecavir 1.0 mg every other day, with supplementation of oral phosphate, vitamin D, and sodium bicarbonate. Following ADV discontinuation, hyperphosphatasemia, hypophosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis gradually improved, and lower limb pain resolved. However, urinary β2-microglobulin remained elevated over the 2-year follow-up, and kidney function remained largely unchanged, indicating irreversible tubular damage from prolonged ADV exposure.
